pages.text: At a roadside stall, a waakye seller lifts the lid of a big ice chest. Steam rises. The rice inside was cooked before sunrise, yet it is still hot at noon. An ice chest is made to keep things cold, so how does it keep food hot? The answer is that the chest does not make heat or cold. It only slows down the movement of thermal energy. Thermal energy always flows from a hotter place to a colder place, and it travels in three ways: conduction, convection, and radiation. Control those three, and you control temperature.

Steam rises.
The rice inside was cooked before sunrise, yet it is still hot at noon.
An ice chest is made to keep things cold, so how does it keep food hot?

It only slows down the movement of thermal energy.

Control those three, and you control temperature.
pages.alt: A food seller at a roadside stall lifting the lid of a large ice chest, with steam rising from the rice inside.

pages.text: Conduction is the transfer of thermal energy through a material, from particle to particle. Leave a metal spoon in hot soup and the handle soon burns your fingers. Metals are good conductors. Wood, plastic, cloth, and air are poor conductors, so we call them insulators. That is why a cooking pot has plastic handles, and why the walls of an ice chest are filled with foam full of trapped air. Convection happens in liquids and gases. Heated water or air expands, becomes lighter, and rises, while cooler water or air sinks to take its place. This circling movement is called a convection current.

Convection happens in liquids and gases.
Heated water or air expands, becomes lighter, and rises, while cooler water or air sinks to take its place.
This circling movement is called a convection current.
pages.alt: A pot of soup on a coal pot with a metal spoon standing in it, and curved arrows showing hot liquid rising and cooler liquid sinking.

pages.text: Radiation is different, because it needs no material at all. Thermal energy from the Sun crosses empty space as infrared rays and warms your skin. Stand beside a coal pot and you feel the same thing. Dark, dull surfaces take in and give out radiation well. Shiny, light surfaces reflect it. Compare two houses at midday. A bare metal roof conducts the Sun’s heat straight into the room below. A thick thatch roof is full of trapped air, so the room stays cooler. A clay water pot cools in another way: water seeps through the clay and evaporates, carrying thermal energy away.

pages.alt: Two houses side by side under a bright sun, one with a bare metal roof and one with a thick thatch roof, and a clay water pot in the shade.

pages.text: Now travel to the far north of Europe, where reindeer live through winters of minus 40 °C. Breathing such air should chill the animal’s lungs, and every warm breath out should waste heat. The reindeer’s nose prevents both. Inside it are thin, curled bones covered with skin that is rich in blood. Cold air flowing in over this large warm surface is heated before it reaches the lungs. On the way out, the warm breath passes over the same surface, which is now cool, and gives back much of its heat and water. A thick coat of hollow hairs traps air around the body.

Cold air flowing in over this large warm surface is heated before it reaches the lungs.

pages.alt: A reindeer standing in deep snow, with a small diagram of the curled passages inside its nose.

pages.text: In northern Ghana, animals have the opposite problem. An elephant in Mole National Park has a huge body that makes a lot of heat, and the air around it is hot. Its ears are the answer. They are large and thin and packed with blood vessels. Warm blood flowing through them loses thermal energy to the air, and flapping the ears moves fresh air across them. Elephants also bathe and spray themselves with mud. People cool down by sweating: as sweat evaporates, it takes thermal energy from the skin. That is why a breeze feels so good on a hot afternoon.

pages.alt: An elephant at a waterhole in Mole National Park with its large ears spread wide.

pages.text: People copy these ideas. A food flask has a double wall with almost no air between the layers, which stops conduction and convection, and a shiny lining that reflects radiation. A fridge has insulation in its walls and door. Builders can keep rooms cool with a ceiling under the roof, light-coloured paint, shade trees, and windows placed so that air flows through. Every one of these saves electricity that would be spent on fans and air conditioners. So the reindeer, the elephant, and the waakye seller all teach one lesson: to manage temperature, manage the transfer of thermal energy.

activities.question: In which direction does thermal energy flow?
options: From a colder place to a hotter place
From a hotter place to a colder place

activities.question: Why are the walls of an ice chest filled with foam?
options: Foam contains trapped air, which is a poor conductor

activities.question: How does a reindeer’s nose save heat?
options: It closes completely in cold weather
Warm breath going out gives heat back to the cool surface inside the nose
It heats the air by burning fat

activities.question: Apply it: A family wants its room under a metal roof to be cooler without using electricity. Which change uses the science in this article?
options: Fit a ceiling under the roof and paint the roof a light colour
Keep every window closed at midday

activities.prompt: Follow one breath through a reindeer’s nose. Put the steps in order.
items: Very cold air enters the nose
The air is warmed as it passes over warm, blood-rich skin
Warm breath flows back out over the cooled surface
Heat and water are given back to the nose before the breath leaves

activities.definition: A material that does not let thermal energy pass through it easily.
distractors: A material that produces heat when it is switched on
A metal that carries heat quickly

glossary.definition: Thermal energy: the energy a substance has because of the movement of its particles; we feel its transfer as heat.
The transfer of thermal energy through a material, from particle to particle.
The transfer of thermal energy by the movement of a heated liquid or gas.
The transfer of thermal energy by rays that can cross empty space.
Materials that do not let thermal energy pass through them easily.
Changes from a liquid into a gas, carrying thermal energy away.
